The Cat Compendium

Frequently Asked Questions

Answers to life's most important questions — all about cats.

Behaviour & Body Language

  • Cats purr by rapidly dilating and constricting the glottis — the part of the larynx that surrounds their vocal cords — during both inhalation and exhalation.

    While purring is often a sign of contentment, cats also purr when stressed, injured, or even giving birth. Some researchers believe the 25–50 Hz vibration frequency may promote bone density and tissue healing.

  • A slow blink — where a cat half-closes its eyes and then reopens them — is a sign of trust and affection. It is often called the "cat kiss."

    Studies have shown that humans who slow-blink back at cats are more likely to receive a slow blink in return. Try it: make soft eye contact and blink slowly — it can build rapport with cats you have just met.

  • Kneading is a behaviour kittens use to stimulate milk flow from their mother. Many cats retain it into adulthood as a self-soothing reflex — you will often see it when a cat is relaxed or settling down to sleep.

    Cats also have scent glands in their paw pads, so kneading a surface or a person is a way of marking something as comforting and familiar.

  • Cats are solitary hunters but social animals. The leading theory is that a cat presenting prey to you is treating you as part of its social group — essentially teaching you to hunt or sharing a resource, much as a mother cat would with her kittens.

    Indoor cats sometimes substitute toys for prey. Accepting the "gift" calmly and without punishment (even if it is a real mouse) preserves the trust your cat is extending to you.

Health & Care

  • Most veterinary associations recommend an annual wellness exam for healthy adult cats (ages 1–10). Senior cats — typically over 10 years old — benefit from twice-yearly check-ups because age-related conditions can progress quickly.

    Kittens need a series of vaccinations and check-ups during their first year. Between scheduled visits, watch for changes in appetite, water intake, litter box habits, or coat quality, which can be early warning signs.

  • Cats are obligate carnivores, meaning their bodies require nutrients — such as taurine, arachidonic acid, and preformed vitamin A — that are found almost exclusively in animal tissue. They cannot synthesise these in sufficient quantities on their own.

    A diet without animal protein puts cats at serious risk of heart disease, vision loss, and neurological damage. If you are concerned about sustainability, look for brands that source protein from insects or laboratory-cultivated meat rather than eliminating animal protein entirely.

  • Cats evolved in arid environments and historically obtained most of their moisture from prey. Their thirst drive is naturally lower than a dog's or a human's, and they can concentrate urine efficiently — though this also makes them prone to kidney and urinary-tract issues if chronically under-hydrated.

<script>
// Collapse all panels at init (content visible in no-JS / reader mode).
document.querySelectorAll('.faq-trigger').forEach((btn) => {
  const panel = btn.closest('h3').nextElementSibling;
  btn.setAttribute('aria-expanded', 'false');
  panel.hidden = true;

  btn.addEventListener('click', () => {
    const open = btn.getAttribute('aria-expanded') === 'true';
    btn.setAttribute('aria-expanded', String(!open));
    panel.hidden = open;
  });

  // Escape collapses and returns focus to the trigger.
  panel.addEventListener('keydown', (e) => {
    if (e.key === 'Escape') {
      btn.setAttribute('aria-expanded', 'false');
      panel.hidden = true;
      btn.focus();
    }
  });
});
  </script>
